CSOs. Options on the curve, not the price.

Every option covered so far in this series references flat price. But the curve itself has vol, and the curve has its own options market. Calendar spread options, CSOs, are options on the spread between two futures months. For storage players, strip hedgers, and curve traders, they are frequently the more precise instrument.

The 5 things to understand about CSOs.

1. What a CSO is
An option on the price difference between two futures months, not on the outright. A June-July WTI CSO call struck at zero pays if June expires above July. Exercise delivers the futures spread, long one month, short the other. Liquidity concentrates in WTI and Henry Hub natgas, the two markets where curve shape is the trade.

2. Why they exist
Spread vol is its own market. Legging vanilla options on each month prices two outright vols joined by a correlation, and adjacent months correlate above 0.95, so the package overcharges for a spread that barely moves most of the time. CSOs price the spread distribution directly. Curve risk gets hedged without paying for outright vol you don't want.

3. Who uses them
Storage players: a CSO call on the carry replicates the storage decision from post 31, the right to capture the spread if it widens past the cost of carry. Producers running strip programs (post 41) hedge the roll risk between the months they hold. Curve traders buy convexity on shape moves that outright options express poorly.

4. The pricing quirks
Spreads cross zero naturally: contango flips to backwardation and back. Lognormal math breaks on an underlying that changes sign, so desks price CSOs on normal-style or spread-specific models. The hidden input is inter-month correlation, and small moves in it swing the mark materially. A CSO book marked on stale correlation is quietly wrong.

5. When they shine
Front-spread stress. April 2020: the WTI front spread collapsed to deeply negative levels while back spreads barely moved. Cold snaps gap winter Henry Hub spreads in days. A CSO bought when the curve is quiet costs a fraction of the vanilla package and pays convex when shape breaks. Cheap convexity for the buyer, an expensive lesson for the seller.

Commodity fundamentals live in the curve more than in the flat price, and CSOs are the instrument that options the curve directly. Storage economics, roll risk, shape views: each gets a cleaner expression than legged vanillas offer. The constraint is liquidity outside energy. Inside energy, they belong in the toolkit.

For anyone hedging curve risk: have you ever priced a CSO against the vanilla package for the same view?
